Solar feed-in tariffs explained

Why the rate you are paid for exports is so much lower than the rate you pay to import — and what that means for how you design and use a system.

Published 1 July 2026Updated 15 October 20266 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

The feed-in tariff is the rate your electricity retailer pays you for each kilowatt hour your system exports to the grid. It is the second-most-quoted number in solar marketing (after the rebate) and the most misunderstood: it is not the price of your energy — it is the price of your surplus, and it is almost always well below what you pay to buy power back.

Why the gap between import and export prices exists

The rate you pay for imported power includes the wholesale cost of energy, but also network charges, metering, environmental program costs and the retailer's margin. When you export, you are selling an energy product into the wholesale market, minus the retailer's costs of handling it. You are selling the energy; you are not selling the transport, the billing or the retail service. That structural difference is why feed-in rates sit well below retail rates in every Australian jurisdiction.

The gap is not a trick — it is the economic reason self-consumption is worth more than exporting, and the reason battery storage exists as a product at all.

How feed-in rates vary

  • By state and regulator — each jurisdiction sets its own rules for what retailers must offer, with minimum or benchmark rates in some states and market-determined rates in others.
  • By retailer and plan — some plans trade a higher feed-in rate for a higher usage rate. The best feed-in tariff is not always the best plan; the total matters.
  • By time of day — some offers now pay more for exports during peak demand periods; these suit batteries that can shift exports to the right window.
  • By network limits — many networks cap either the size of inverter allowed to export or the volume of export at certain times. Generation above the cap is curtailed, not sold.

What a low feed-in tariff actually means for design

  • Self-consumption is the priority: a kilowatt hour used on site saves the full retail rate, while the same hour exported earns the feed-in rate — often a small fraction of it.
  • Storage converts low-value exports into high-value evening supply, which is exactly the gap a battery is designed to arbitrage.
  • Oversizing to 'make money from exports' is a weak strategy where feed-in rates are low; arrays sized near consumption perform better.
  • Load-shifting is free feed-in optimisation: running the pool, hot water or EV charger in the middle of the day means fewer exports and more avoided imports.

Do not buy a system for the feed-in tariff

Feed-in rates are set by retailers and regulators and can change with little notice. A system whose business case depends on a high export rate is a bet on policy and market conditions, not an investment in your own consumption. The durable value is in the kilowatt hours you use yourself.

Checking the current rates

Feed-in rates are published in every plan's terms and in the government comparison service Energy Made Easy, which lets you compare offers using your actual usage data. If you already have solar, the service uses your export volumes too — which is the only honest way to compare plans with different feed-in rates.

Key takeaways

  • Feed-in tariffs pay for exports; they are not what you pay for imports.
  • The import–export gap is structural: retail rates include network and service costs that exports do not.
  • Self-consumption saves the full retail rate; exports earn the tariff — the difference is the whole game.
  • Check export limits on your network — some generation may never reach the grid.
  • Compare plans on total value using your own data via Energy Made Easy, not on headline feed-in rates.
